```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
source('latex-figure.R')
```

The number of sunspots rises and falls in a cycle of about 11 years. This
article fits that cycle as a damped oscillator, a second order model, to the
yearly counts from 1700 to 1988. It shows how to model a single subject,
what a pair of complex eigenvalues of the drift matrix means, and how to fit
the same model by Bayesian sampling with priors chosen for the data.

```{r libs}
library(ctsem)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Data

ctsem takes long format data with an id column, a time column and the
observed variables. Here there is one subject, the sun.

```{r data}
ssdat <- data.frame(id = 1, time = as.numeric(time(sunspot.year)),
  sunspots = as.numeric(sunspot.year))
head(ssdat)
```

```{r plotdata, fig.height = 3}
ggplot(ssdat, aes(time, sunspots)) + geom_line() + theme_bw()
```

# A damped oscillator

A first order model lets a process return towards its equilibrium after a
shock, but it cannot overshoot and swing back. To get a cycle, the model
needs a second latent process, the rate of change of the first. Call them
`level` and `velocity`:

- the level changes at the rate given by the velocity, so `DRIFT[1, 2]` is
  fixed to 1 and the level's own auto effect to 0;
- the velocity changes according to the level (`a21`) and to itself
  (`a22`). A negative `a21` pulls a high level back down, and a negative
  `a22` damps the swings;
- random shocks act on the velocity only, so `DIFFUSION` has one free cell;
- only the level is measured (`LAMBDA = c(1, 0)`), with an intercept `m1`
  and measurement error.

With the intercept on the measurement, the continuous time intercept `CINT`
is fixed to 0. By default the intercepts and starting values vary over
subjects, which one subject cannot show, so the last line turns that off.

```{r model}
ssmodel <- ctModel(type = 'ct',
  manifestNames = 'sunspots',
  latentNames = c('level', 'velocity'),
  LAMBDA = c(1, 0),
  DRIFT = c(0, 1,
    'a21', 'a22'),
  MANIFESTMEANS = 'm1',
  CINT = 0,
  DIFFUSION = c(0, 0,
    0, 'diffusion'))
ssmodel$pars$indvarying <- FALSE
```

`ctModelLatex(ssmodel)` writes the model out as equations and opens them as a
pdf:

```{r latex-model, echo = FALSE, out.width = '100%'}
latexFigure(ssmodel)
```

`ctModelHigherOrder()` adds second order dynamics to an existing model, which
is quicker for a model with many processes.

# Fitting

```{r fit}
fit <- ctFit(ssdat, ssmodel, cores = 2)
```

With one subject the variance of the starting values (`T0VAR`) cannot be
estimated either, so `ctFit()` fixes it to a small value and says so in a
message. It would also have removed the random effects if the model had
kept them.

```{r summary}
summary(fit)$popmeans
```

Both drift parameters are negative. The level is pulled back towards its
mean of about `r round(summary(fit)$popmeans['m1', 'mean'])` sunspots, and
the swings are damped.

The drift matrix's eigenvalues say more. A pair of complex eigenvalues means
the process oscillates. The imaginary part gives the period of the cycle, and
the real part how quickly the amplitude of a cycle decays when no new shocks
arrive:

```{r eigen}
drift <- ctSummaryMatrices(fit)$estimate$DRIFT
drift
ev <- eigen(drift)$values
ev
2 * pi / abs(Im(ev[1]))   # period, in years
log(2) / abs(Re(ev[1]))   # half-life of the amplitude, in years
```

The estimated period is `r round(2 * pi / abs(Im(ev[1])), 1)` years, close
to the known sunspot cycle. Without new shocks, the amplitude of a cycle
would halve in about `r round(log(2) / abs(Re(ev[1])), 1)` years. The random
shocks to the velocity keep the cycle going, and make each cycle's height
different.

`ctDiscretePars()` shows the same thing as the effect over time of a one unit
shock to each process. A shock to the level swings it below zero after about
five years and back up after ten:

```{r discrete}
ctDiscretePars(fit, times = seq(0, 30, by = 0.5), plot = TRUE)
```

# Predicted and smoothed states

`ctPredict()` gives the model's predictions for each time, here every 0.1
years. The predicted values (`yprior`) use only the earlier observations,
so they show what the model would have forecast. The plot is a ggplot, so
`coord_cartesian()` can zoom in on a few cycles:

```{r predict}
ctPredict(fit, timestep = 0.1, plot = TRUE, kalmanvec = c('y', 'yprior')) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(1900, 1960))
```

Between observations the forecast follows the cycle, and its uncertainty
grows until the next observation arrives. The smoothed states
(`etasmooth`) use all observations, before and after each time. They give
the best estimate of the level and of its velocity, which is not observed:

```{r smooth}
ctPredict(fit, timestep = 0.1, plot = TRUE, kalmanvec = 'etasmooth') +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(1900, 1960))
```

The velocity is highest while the level rises fastest, and crosses zero at
each peak and trough of the level.

# Bayesian estimation

`priors = TRUE` adds a prior to every parameter, and `optimize = FALSE`
samples the posterior. Each parameter is a transform of a standard normal
raw parameter, so the transform sets the prior:

```{r transforms}
ssmodel$pars[!is.na(ssmodel$pars$param), c('matrix', 'param', 'transform')]
```

The defaults suit data centred near zero. `m1`, the
mean number of sunspots, gets a normal prior with mean 0 and standard
deviation 10, while the data have a mean of about 50. A prior predictive
check shows what such priors imply. `ctGenerate(fromPriors = TRUE)` draws
parameters from the priors and generates data with the design of `ssdat`:

```{r priorpred-default}
prior <- ctGenerate(ssmodel, fromPriors = TRUE, datastruct = ssdat,
  nsamples = 50)
dim(prior$Y)   # draws by rows of data by variables
```

The second field of a parameter's string sets its transform.
`'m1|param*20+50'` gives `m1` a normal prior with mean 50 and standard
deviation 20, and `'t0_level|param*50'` lets the level start up to about 100
from that mean:

```{r adjust}
ssmodel2 <- ctModel(type = 'ct',
  manifestNames = 'sunspots',
  latentNames = c('level', 'velocity'),
  LAMBDA = c(1, 0),
  DRIFT = c(0, 1,
    'a21', 'a22'),
  T0MEANS = c('t0_level|param*50', 't0_velocity'),
  MANIFESTMEANS = 'm1|param*20+50',
  CINT = 0,
  DIFFUSION = c(0, 0,
    0, 'diffusion'))
ssmodel2$pars$indvarying <- FALSE
prior2 <- ctGenerate(ssmodel2, fromPriors = TRUE, datastruct = ssdat,
  nsamples = 50)
```

```{r priorpred-plot, fig.height = 4.5}
priorlines <- function(gen, label) {
  data.frame(priors = label,
    time = rep(ssdat$time, each = dim(gen$Y)[1]),
    draw = rep(seq_len(dim(gen$Y)[1]), times = nrow(ssdat)),
    sunspots = c(gen$Y[, , 1]))
}
pp <- rbind(priorlines(prior, 'default priors'),
  priorlines(prior2, 'adjusted priors'))
pp$priors <- factor(pp$priors, levels = c('default priors', 'adjusted priors'))
ggplot(pp, aes(time, sunspots)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = draw), colour = 'red', alpha = .2) +
  geom_line(data = ssdat, linewidth = .7) +
  facet_wrap(~priors) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-150, 250)) +
  theme_bw()
```

Under the default priors the series is centred near zero. The adjusted priors
cover the data and still allow a wide range of other series. Some draws grow
without bound, because the prior on `a21` allows positive values, which push
the level away from its mean. The data rule those out. With 289 years
of data the priors matter little for the dynamics, but a prior far from the
data can slow the sampler and, with less data, move the estimates.

```{r sample}
sfit <- ctFit(ssdat, ssmodel2, priors = TRUE, optimize = FALSE, cores = 2)
summary(sfit)$popmeans
```

The posterior means are close to the maximum likelihood estimates above.
`n_eff` is the effective number of independent draws, and `Rhat` near 1 says
the chains agree. `ctPlotPosterior()` compares each parameter's posterior with
its prior:

```{r postplot, fig.height = 6}
ctPlotPosterior(sfit)
```

`ctGenerateFromFit()` generates new data from the fitted model, with the
times of the original data. With `fullposterior = TRUE` each data set uses a
different draw from the posterior. Here are three, against the data in black:

```{r postpred}
gen <- ctGenerateFromFit(sfit, nsamples = 3, fullposterior = TRUE)
post <- data.frame(time = rep(ssdat$time, each = 3),
  draw = factor(rep(1:3, times = nrow(ssdat))),
  sunspots = c(gen$generated$Y[, , 1]))
ggplot(post, aes(time, sunspots)) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = draw), alpha = .7) +
  geom_line(data = ssdat, linewidth = .7) +
  theme_bw()
```

The generated series cycle at about the same rate as the data, but less
regularly, and they often go below zero, which sunspot counts cannot. The
data also rise faster than they fall, which a linear model cannot produce. A
model of the square root of the counts, or a count measurement model
(`manifesttype = 3`, see `vignette('measurement-models')`), would be a next
step.
